en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 31 [Tibetan & Sanskrit, 34] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
[1214'] Now I shall describe another procedure, the sequence of the rite for the opening of the rainy season:
upon a beautiful eight-petaled lotus, filled with a pericarp and filaments.
In the center there is the Great Vajra, together with Draṣṭa and Utkatabhairava;
he has eight arms, four faces, and three eyes, and is terrifyingly formidable.
He is intent on brandishing a vajra and holds a noose with his index finger.
He holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, wields a goad and a trident,
wears a garment of Indra’s hide, and the ḍamaru drum is remembered as the eighth [attribute].
He stands in the ālīḍha posture, treading upon Varuṇa, who is overwhelmed with fear.
His matted hair is bound with a crescent moon and adorned with a double-vajra;
his body is decorated with the six mudrās and embellished with a garland of severed heads;
he is clothed in a tiger skin and wears a supreme crown of skulls.
With his lower lip bitten and distorted, he gazes with an angry look.

On the eight-petaled lotus, one should draw the eight Naga kings: Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, Karkoṭaka, and Navatapta. They are white, blue, red, green, yellow, smoky-grey, pale-grey, and greenish-yellow respectively. With palms joined in *añjali*, they gaze at the face of the Blessed One, seeking his command. One should visualize them as terrified and trembling.
The Blessed One has a dark blue body, terrifying even to fear itself;
his right face is smoky red, while his left is greenish-grey.
With an upward-facing face, a garuḍa-head, deformed and terrifying,
red in color with the brilliance of the sun, possessing a luster equal to twelve suns,
and embraced around the neck by Vārāhī, who is well-enveloped up to her knees.

Alternatively, one should visualize that Mahāsukha as twelve-armed, embraced by the Goddess who holds a *kartṛkā*, the head of Brahmā, a vajra, and a bell; he presses down upon her lower lip. She is naked, with loose hair, three-eyed, and radiant with girdles.
The Nāgas [beheld] her whose body was as fierce as Jāmbūnada gold, established in non-dual yoga; Varuṇa together with his wife [beheld] Varuṇa, whose body was white and fierce, seeking their command.
In the heart, one should place the Wisdom-Krodhas, born from their respective colors, weapons, and faces; and having placed *phuṃ*, *ṇaṃ*, and *huṃ* in that heart, as well as body, speech, and mind,
one should likewise place *phuṃ*, *ṇaṃ*, *ūṃ*, and *sva* in the hearts of the Nāgas.
One should recite the mantra born [of it] according to the rule with wrathful speech.
Whether on a riverbank, at the ocean, at a well, or likewise at a lake, or in a large pond, a small pool, or a cistern— one should perform the recitation while filled with wrath.
Alternatively, one should begin the practice of meditation and recitation in the abode of the nāgas.
Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru ka puṇye nāgād varṣaya 2 hūṃ hūṃ ḍākinījālasamvara hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Thus, joined with recitation and meditation four times a day for one thousand repetitions,
it will certainly cause rain upon all the earth within seven nights.

The yogi should perform worship and fire-offerings (homa) accompanied by dance and song, and recite the mantra of the Naga King while maintaining a diet and seat consisting of milk. He should bathe [the deity] with milk according to the ritual rules and likewise offer milk as the oblation in the fire.
Having made fuel from milk-tree wood and using sacrificial sticks produced from milk trees, one should offer oblations together with [milk]; jars filled with milk should be offered,
and an offering accompanied by milk should be presented to the ten directions.
Oṃ aṃ to Ananta, phuṃ ṇaṃ (kṣīṃ) hūṃ svāhā.
HŪṂ VAṂ! O Varuṇa, lords of the nāgas, cause the nāgas to send rain! PHUṂ ÑAṂ PHUṂ SVĀHĀ!
Thus one should mutter with a wrathful mind; one should perform that recitation for all [beings].

Having restrained the senses, subsisting on milk, observing silence while eating old porridge and rice, and focusing upon this chapter (*paṭala*), if one performs one hundred thousand recitations facing away [from the object], he becomes intoxicated and turns his face toward [the practitioner]. By means of the disciple’s speech, he causes rain to fall; of this there is no doubt. One should act accordingly.

Having consecrated mustard-seed water twenty-one times in a silver vessel, one should bathe a Buddha image with scented water mixed with milk along with the threefold world (*sāṃdhātuka*). Having fashioned an image of a *nāga*, one should make it from earth taken from both banks of a river; then, facing west, one should sprinkle its head and subsequently cast it into the river. At that very moment, it releases a downpour of rain over the entire Jambudvīpa.
The earth becomes abundant with crops and filled with wealth and grain; all sentient beings shall dwell in the touch of happiness.

Having fashioned a physical form according to the tantra that displays mutual anger, one visualizes Herukavajra within its heart and causes rain to fall. By reciting the mantra over a trident and ascending a mountain, one brings down the thunderbolt.
"Having recited over the ḍamaru drum, one causes the burning by fire;
having recited over the noose, one draws [the victim] forth;
having recited over the skull-cup, one draws forth blood."
"Having recited over an axe, one kills;
having recited over a khaṭvāṅga staff, one becomes tranquil."
"By reciting *kaṃtti*, one protects the three worlds; by reciting *māma*, one protects [the self]; by reciting *muṇḍa*, one raises the dead;
and by reciting *vajra* and brandishing it, the accomplishment of *pātāla* (the underworld) is attained."
Having recited over a bell, one causes it to ring.
Having recited over an elephant hide, one leaps into the sky at the boundary of the *samaya* and travels three million *yojanas*; then one returns again.
Having recited over the six mudrās and rubbed them upon the body, one becomes invisible; one may wander upon the surface of the earth and dwell there as one pleases.
In the *Abhidhānottarottara*, the chapter on the ritual procedure for the rain-retreat (*varṣāpaṇavidhi*)... [1242']
